01.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai were sitting and drinking wine when a man came by, and they asked him to pour for them. After he poured, it turned out he was a gentile. One of the two Sages forbade the wine even for any benefit, while the other allowed it even for drinking. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said both were right: one assumed the gentile thought such great Sages must be drinking wine and might have poured it to an idol, the other that he assumed they were drinking liquor, since they would never ask a gentile to serve them wine.
01.why: The Gemara has been debating how strictly to treat wine a gentile touched by accident, after Abaye refuted Rava's lenient view; this incident adds a case where the gentile's own assumptions decide whether he meant to offer it to an idol.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza
people.about: One of the two Sages drinking wine; one of them forbade it and one permitted it.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai
people.about: The other Sage drinking wine with Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage who later judged that both rulings were proper and explained each one.

terms.meaning: Offering wine to an idol by pouring it out. Wine a gentile may have poured for an idol was forbidden to Jews, even for selling.
Any use or profit from something, such as selling it, not only eating or drinking it.

02.note: Rabbi Tarfon swore, "I will bury my sons" if he had not heard from his teachers a distinction between collecting a sacrifice's blood and sprinkling it, but he could not remember what it was. Rabbi Akiva offered to explain, and listed three differences between the two acts. Rabbi Tarfon swore by the Temple service that Akiva had not strayed left or right from what he had heard, and said: "Akiva, anyone who leaves you is like one who leaves his life."
02.why: The mishna says wrong intent while collecting the blood disqualifies an offering; Rabbi Akiva's explanation here says it does not, so the Gemara cites the exchange as a contradiction, which Rava then resolves by distinguishing two kinds of intent.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who remembered hearing a rule from his teachers but could not explain it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who worked out the rule on his own, matching what Rabbi Tarfon had heard.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.
Literally "cutting off": a punishment from Heaven, often understood as early death or loss of one's place among the people.
Two steps in a Temple sacrifice: a priest catches the animal's blood in a vessel, then sprinkles it on the altar.

03.note: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana were sitting together when a man passed by wearing a cloak made entirely of sky-blue wool, with white and sky-blue ritual fringes that were wound all the way down, with no loose strands hanging. Rav said the cloak was beautiful but the fringes were not. Rabba bar bar Hana said both the cloak and the fringes were beautiful.
03.why: The Gemara has just set rules for how the fringe strings are wound; their two remarks become a disagreement over whether fringes must also have loose strings hanging below the windings, which the Gemara then traces to two verses.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who said the cloak was beautiful but the fringes were not.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rav who said both the cloak and the fringes were beautiful.

terms.meaning: Strings the Torah requires on the corners of a four-cornered garment (tzitzit), including a sky-blue thread.
A blue dye (tekhelet) the Torah requires for one thread of the fringes.
Sets of coils wrapped around the fringe strings near the garment.

04.note: The Sages told Rabbi Perida that Rabbi Ezra, a descendant of Ezra the Scribe through a long line of famous Sages, was waiting at his gate. Rabbi Perida asked why they were listing his ancestors: a man of Torah is worthy on his own, but a man of lineage without Torah, "better for fire to devour him" than enter. Told that Ezra was a man of Torah, he let him in. Seeing Ezra was troubled, Rabbi Perida taught a homily praising the Patriarchs as those whom God credits. Hearing the word "excellent" (addir), Rabbi Ezra replied with a series of wordplay homilies on addir, yadid (beloved), "good" and "this," each tying Moses, Solomon, Abraham, the Torah, the Temple, God and Israel together.
04.why: Rabbi Perida has just appeared in the discussion asking where meal offerings get their rule against leavening, so the Gemara attaches this incident about him.

people.name: Rabbi Perida
people.about: A Sage at whose house Rabbi Ezra waited; he insisted that Torah learning, not lineage, makes a man worthy.

people.name: Rabbi Ezra
people.about: A Sage descended from Ezra the Scribe, who answered Rabbi Perida with homilies of his own.

people.name: Ezra
people.about: Ezra the Scribe, Rabbi Ezra's ancestor.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A Sage in Rabbi Ezra's family line, descended from Ezra the Scribe.

people.name: Rabbi Avtolus
people.about: Rabbi Ezra's grandfather, a descendant of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

terms.meaning: A sermon-like reading of Bible verses that draws a lesson from wording, often through wordplay.
Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the founding fathers of the Jewish people.

05.note: Three women brought three pairs of birds as offerings. One said hers was "for my ziva," one "for my yamma," and one "for my ona." The Sages took all three to mean bleeding and purification, so each would bring a sin offering and a burnt offering. Mordekhai suggested instead that one had been in danger from a flow, one at sea (yam), and one through her eye (ayin), so all three were thanksgiving burnt offerings. It was checked, and Mordekhai was found to be right.
05.why: The Gemara has just told how Mordekhai decoded a deaf-mute's gestures to find grain for the Temple; this is a further example of his skill with words, and leads to identifying him with Petahya, who was in charge of bird offerings.

people.name: Mordekhai
people.about: A Sage who read the women's words differently from the other Sages and was found to be right.

terms.meaning: Pairs of pigeons or doves brought as offerings, for example by a woman after certain kinds of bleeding.
A woman with a discharge of blood outside her normal period, who must bring an offering when she is purified.
A sin offering atones for a specific state or wrong; a burnt offering is burned whole on the altar and can also be a voluntary gift.

06.note: Rabbi Tarfon sat puzzling over why meal offerings from new grain brought before the omer are unfit, while those brought before the two loaves are fit. Yehuda ben Nehemya answered him with a distinction, Rabbi Tarfon fell silent, and the young man's face lit up. Rabbi Akiva said to him: "Yehuda, has your face brightened because you answered the elder? I will be astonished if your life is long." Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Ilai reported that this happened two weeks before Passover; when he came back for Shavuot and asked about Yehuda ben Nehemya, he was told he had died.
06.why: The mishna rules that offerings from new grain brought before the omer are unfit but those brought between the omer and the two loaves are fit; the incident gives the reasoning for that difference, which Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak then extends to fruit.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: An elder Sage who raised the question and fell silent at the answer.

people.name: Yehuda ben Nehemya
people.about: A Sage who answered Rabbi Tarfon and looked pleased; he died soon afterward.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who rebuked Yehuda ben Nehemya for gloating over answering the elder.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ilai
people.about: A Sage who tells when the incident happened and that Yehuda ben Nehemya died.

terms.meaning: A measure of new barley offered in the Temple on the second day of Passover; only after it may the new crop be eaten.
Two wheat loaves offered on Shavuot, after which the new crop may be used for Temple offerings.
An offering of flour, usually mixed with oil, brought in the Temple.

07.note: Shimon HaTzaddik, the High Priest, foresaw his death: each Yom Kippur an old man in white had entered the Holy of Holies with him and left with him, but this year he was in black and did not leave. He died after Sukkot, naming his son Onias as successor. In Rabbi Meir's telling, Onias's older brother Shimi, jealous, tricked Onias into a tunic and ribbon and told the priests it was a vow to his lover; the priests wanted to kill Onias, who fled to Alexandria and built an altar for idol worship. Rabbi Yehuda says it was the reverse: Onias declined the post, then grew jealous and played the trick on Shimi; when exposed he fled to Alexandria and built an altar to God. The Sages drew a lesson about jealousy over high office.
07.why: The mishna implies the temple of Onias in Egypt was not for idol worship; this baraita is cited because Rabbi Yehuda's version supports that view, while Rabbi Meir's says it was.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A High Priest who foresaw his own death and named his son Onias to succeed him.

people.name: Onias
people.about: Son of Shimon HaTzaddik, who built an altar in Alexandria in Egypt.

people.name: Shimi
people.about: Onias's brother, two and a half years older than him.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage whose version says Onias's altar was for idol worship.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who says the incident went otherwise and Onias's altar was for God.

terms.meaning: The innermost room of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, on Yom Kippur.
The blessing the priests recite over the people; in the Temple it was said with God's own name.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

08.note: Rabbi Zeira and Rav Asi stopped at an inn in the town of Ya'ei and were served eggs cooked in wine. Rabbi Zeira did not eat; Rav Asi did. Rabbi Zeira asked whether he was not worried that the wine might be untithed produce, and Rav Asi said it had not occurred to him. Rabbi Zeira reasoned that God would not let a righteous man stumble into eating forbidden food, looked into it, and found a teaching that a mixture containing such doubtful produce is permitted.
08.why: The Gemara is returning to its earlier claim that the righteous do not come to mishaps; this story shows it at work, and the Gemara then questions whether the Sages really exempted such mixtures.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who refused the eggs and then found a ruling that showed his companion did nothing wrong.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: A Sage who ate the eggs without thinking about whether the wine was tithed.

terms.meaning: Produce bought from someone not trusted to have set aside the required tithes, so it must be tithed again out of doubt.
Portions of produce the Torah requires to be given to priests, Levites or the poor, or eaten in Jerusalem.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

09.note: Rava would check an arrow for Rabbi Yona bar Tahlifa to make sure it had no notches, and the arrow was shot and slaughtered a bird in flight. The Gemara asks whether the arrow might have cut the neck from the back, and answers that the feathers at the front of the neck were seen to be undone, showing the cut came from the front.
09.why: The Gemara has just derived from "a sharpened arrow" that slaughter must be a drawing motion, like an arrow's flight; this incident shows a bird actually slaughtered by an arrow.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who checked the arrow for nicks before it was shot.

people.name: Rabbi Yona bar Tahlifa
people.about: The Sage for whom the arrow was checked and the bird slaughtered.

terms.meaning: Kosher slaughter, which must cut the windpipe and gullet with a smooth drawing cut from the front of the neck.
The windpipe and gullet, the two passages that must be cut in kosher slaughter.
Cutting the neck from the back toward the front, which is not valid.

09.flag: The English names Rava as shooting the arrow while the AFTER discussion treats Rabbi Yona bar Tahlifa as the slaughterer; the note leaves the shooter unnamed, worth checking.

10.note: Moths got into Rabbi Hiyya's flax, and he went to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to ask how to get rid of them. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him to take a bird and slaughter it over the tub of water where the flax was soaking, because the moths would smell the blood and leave.
10.why: The mishna exempts from covering the blood one who kills a bird by stabbing or tearing; the Gemara asks how Rabbi Hiyya could keep the blood of a slaughtered bird, which must be covered, and answers that he was told to kill it in a way that brings no such duty.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage whose flax was infested with moths.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leading Sage Rabbi Hiyya asked for advice.

terms.meaning: A plant soaked in water to make linen fibers.

11.note: Rav Beruna and Rav Hananel, students of Rav, were eating together while Rav Yeiva the Elder served them. They asked him for a cup of wine to say Grace after Meals over, then changed their minds and asked for a cup to drink. Rav Yeiva told them that Rav taught: once someone asks for the cup for Grace after Meals, he may not drink more wine without first saying a new blessing.
11.why: Rabbi Hanina said one blessing covers slaughtering an animal and a bird even with covering blood in between; Ravina cites this meal as a case where a pause requires a new blessing, and the Gemara rejects the comparison.

people.name: Rav Beruna
people.about: A student of Rav, eating with Rav Hananel.

people.name: Rav Hananel
people.about: A student of Rav, eating with Rav Beruna.

people.name: Rav Yeiva the Elder
people.about: The man serving them, who reported Rav's rule.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher of the two students, whose rule Rav Yeiva quotes.

terms.meaning: The blessings said after eating bread, often recited over a cup of wine.

12.note: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya was peeling the membranes off a spleen for Levi, son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya, cutting only from the upper surface. Levi told him to go further down. Levi's father arrived and said that Levi's maternal grandfather, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, taught in Rav's name that the Torah forbids only the membranes on the thick upper surface. Levi cited a baraita implying that membranes on all sides are forbidden, and his father answered: if that baraita is taught, it is taught.
12.why: The Gemara has just listed the spleen's membrane among those forbidden for their fat; the incident raises how much of it is forbidden, and the Gemara then reconciles two baraitot by the upper and lower parts of the spleen.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya
people.about: The man peeling the membranes from the spleen.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya, who wanted more of the membrane removed.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: Levi's father, who quoted a ruling from Levi's grandfather.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Levi's mother's father, who taught a ruling in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who reported the baraita Levi cited.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.
Literally "cutting off": a punishment from Heaven for certain serious sins, such as eating forbidden fat.
Certain fats of cattle, sheep and goats that the Torah forbids eating.

13.note: In a year of famine, a man invited three guests and had only three eggs to set before them. His son came in, and each guest in turn gave the boy his egg. The father came and found the boy with one egg in his mouth and two in his hand, and in anger struck him to the ground, and the boy died. The mother, seeing this, went up to the roof, fell and died, and then the father did the same and died.
13.why: The baraita has just ruled that guests may not give the host's children food from the table without his permission; this incident is its warning, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov notes that three lives were lost over it.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

14.note: A Jewish butcher said to a man he had quarrelled with: had you made peace with me yesterday, I would have given you a cut of the fattened bull I prepared. The man answered that he had eaten the finest of that bull anyway; a certain gentile had bought it and fed it to him. The butcher said he had prepared two bulls, and the one the man ate was a tereifa, which is why he sold it to a gentile. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, hearing of it, said: because of this imbecile, should we forbid all the meat in the gentile butcher shops of the city?
14.why: The Gemara is discussing selling non-kosher meat to gentiles, and whether meat found with a gentile can be trusted where Jewish butchers work; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reaction fits his own ruling that such meat is permitted.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The leading Sage, who refused to forbid all gentile butcher meat because of this case.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect, which may not be eaten by Jews even if properly slaughtered.
A non-Jew.

15.note: While Rav lived in Babylonia, Rabbi Yohanan in the Land of Israel addressed letters to him as "our Master." After Rav died, he wrote to Shmuel as "our colleague." Stung, Shmuel sent him calculations of leap years for sixty years, which did not impress him, then explanations of doubtful cases of tereifot that filled thirteen camel-loads. Rabbi Yohanan said, "I have a Master in Babylonia," and planned to visit, but first asked a child for his verse; the child recited "Now Samuel was dead." Rabbi Yohanan concluded Shmuel had died and did not go. The Gemara comments that Shmuel was alive; the sign came so Rabbi Yohanan would be spared the hard journey.
15.why: The Gemara has just said that Rav, Shmuel and Rabbi Yohanan each looked for signs, Rabbi Yohanan by asking a child for his verse; this story shows him doing it.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage in the Land of Israel who corresponded with the Sages of Babylonia.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage in Babylonia whom Rabbi Yohanan addressed as "our Master."

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage in Babylonia who set out to show Rabbi Yohanan he was his master.

terms.meaning: Years to which a month is added so the Jewish calendar keeps in step with the seasons.
Animals with defects that make them forbidden to eat; deciding doubtful cases takes great expertise.

16.note: When Rabbi Zeira moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, he found Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi eating bread with their hands covered by worn pieces of wineskin instead of washing them. He asked how two great men could misread the incident of Rav and Shmuel, since Rav had told Shmuel he did wash his hands and only used a cloth because he was delicate.
16.why: The Gemara is asking whether covering the hands can replace washing before bread; it then explains that Rabbi Zeira had forgotten a ruling allowing this for priests, which Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel and questioned his colleagues' practice.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage in the Land of Israel eating with covered hands.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage eating with Rabbi Ami in the same way.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who, in an earlier incident, ate with a cloth after washing.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who had questioned Rav about eating with a cloth.

terms.meaning: The ritual rinsing of hands required before eating bread.

17.note: Meat from a properly slaughtered animal was salted for Rav Mari bar Rahel together with tereifa meat, in a perforated vessel. He came to Rava to ask whether the kosher meat was now forbidden. Rava ruled from the verse "These are the unclean to you" that not only the forbidden flesh is prohibited but also its juices, gravy and spices, so even while the kosher meat was giving off its blood it absorbed the juices of the forbidden meat.
17.why: Rav Nahman has just ruled that fish salted with birds absorb their blood even in a perforated vessel; this case asks whether kosher meat absorbs from forbidden meat salted beside it, and the Gemara then tests Rava's answer against Shmuel's rule and a baraita about fish.

people.name: Rav Mari bar Rahel
people.about: The man whose meat was salted together with tereifa meat.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the case.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect, which may not be eaten by Jews even if properly slaughtered.
Meat is salted to draw out its blood, which Jews may not eat.
A container with holes, so the blood and juices drain away instead of pooling.

18.note: Rava and Rav Safra visited Mar Yohana, who prepared a calf for them. Rava asked Mar Yohana's attendant, a priest, to grant them the priestly portions so he could eat tongue with mustard. Rava ate; Rav Safra did not. Afterward a verse of rebuke was read to Rav Safra in a dream, and he asked Rav Yosef whether he had broken his ruling. Rav Yosef said no: his ruling applied only to a priest giving freely to a needy scholar, not an attendant pressured before a host's guest, and Rava was not poor. The rebuke was meant for Rava, the Gemara explains, who was not granted such a dream himself.
18.why: Rav Yosef has just ruled that a priest may assign his gifts to a poor Torah scholar; this incident sets the limits of that ruling.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who ate the priestly portions given by the attendant.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage who refused to eat them and later had a dream of rebuke.

people.name: Mar Yohana
people.about: The host who prepared a calf for his guests.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage whose ruling was at issue and who explained the dream.

terms.meaning: Parts of a slaughtered animal (the foreleg, jaw with tongue, and stomach) that are given to a priest.

19.note: Rav Kahana said he saw the pigeons of Herod's breed standing in sixteen rows, each a mil wide, calling "My master, my master." One pigeon was silent, and another told it, "Blind one, say: My master, my master." It answered, "Blind one, you should say: My master, my slave," since Herod was a slave and not a true king. That pigeon was taken to the slaughterhouse and slaughtered.
19.why: The mishna's domesticated pigeons may be named for King Herod, who bred them; Rav Kahana's account follows that explanation, and the Gemara then says the scene was produced by witchcraft rather than being mere talk.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who reported seeing the pigeons himself.

people.name: Herod
people.about: The king whose pigeons these were; the pigeon calls him a slave rather than a king.

terms.meaning: A distance of roughly a kilometer.

20.note: Levi bar Simon gave Rav Yehuda the yield of his dovecote, the fledglings and eggs in it. Rav Yehuda came to Shmuel and told him of it. Shmuel told him to go and bang on the dovecote so the birds would rise up, and then he could acquire them. The story does not say what happened next.
20.why: The Gemara has been asking when the owner of a courtyard or dovecote acquires the eggs in it; it then asks why banging was needed and explains that Levi bar Simon himself had not yet acquired the new young.

people.name: Levi bar Simon
people.about: The owner of the dovecote, who gave its yield to Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The man who received the dovecote's yield and asked Shmuel how to take it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who told Rav Yehuda to bang on the dovecote.

terms.meaning: A structure where pigeons nest.
Take legal ownership, which in Jewish law requires a recognized act, not only words.
